claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS only (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
Multi-cloud is nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
SST was originally built on top of AWS CDK, which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python (table marks language support as limited), while Pulumi supports any programming language.
With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises platforms.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because of direct execution versus CloudFormation.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster infrastructure experience.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi supports extensibility through custom providers and dynamic components (dynamic providers).
Pulumi executes infrastructure code directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for infrastructure deployments.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ and supports advanced deployment workflows.
The Pulumi docs page on CloudFormation comparison has a section anchored 'what-is-aws-cloudformation'.
The Pulumi docs page on AWS CDK comparison has a section anchored 'what-is-aws-cdk'.
An AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/ describing Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifying 'day one' tasks.
An on-demand workshop 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new SST engine for deploying SST applications, deploying components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
An embedded YouTube video with ID LXxJ9XMXC6o exists relating to CDK and CloudFormation limitations.
SST (Serverless Stack) is a framework that aims to bridge the gap between application developers and infrastructure management.
SST's team expanded beyond AWS to explore other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and added support for new providers after moving to Pulumi.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
The SST team has repeatedly said, about their own architecture, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST docs 'What is SST' say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

SST's published platform/package.json depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (@pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, @pulumiverse/vercel).
The SST repository is now at anomalyco/sst (formerly sst/sst) on GitHub, with platform/package.json on the dev branch.

In SST deploys, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.

Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," with official Nitric providers built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang's Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) takes "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result; Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.

Most SST users never write Pulumi code; resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has more GitHub stars than SST.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and its release cadence has not changed because of the opencode work.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.

Pulumi Cloud offers cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST users are running Pulumi's engine, and Pulumi Cloud, policy as code and components work with the same engine SST uses.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.

The linked pages exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/.
The post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
SST is a strong fit for an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together.
